title: Medicare Advantage Companies Bank Billions in Bonuses
author: Brandon Novick
content:
After [stealing](https://cepr.net/publications/new-research-reveals-millions-
will-lose-medicare-advantage-coverage-this-year/)
[hundreds](https://cepr.net/publications/does-this-trump-proposal-end-the-
insurance-industrys-medicare-gravy-train/) of billions of dollars from
taxpayers, insurance companies in the Medicare Advantage program are going to
face significant government action. And significant government action, in this
case, means that the federal government is going to award an
[estimated](https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-will-spend-more-
than-13-billion-on-the-medicare-advantage-quality-bonus-program-in-2026/) $13
billion to the insurers in bonus payments.

These bonuses are not officially a direct reward for insurance companies
exploiting taxpayers, but they are emblematic of a completely broken system.

Quality bonuses in the Medicare Advantage program are meant to reward insurers
for providing high-quality plans to seniors and others who qualify for
Medicare. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) maintains a five-
star quality rating system, and the agency awards bonuses for plans that earn
at least four out of five stars. As currently structured, this system was
[created](https://www.congress.gov/111/plaws/publ148/PLAW-111publ148.pdf) by
the Affordable Care Act in 2012.

For 2026, the stars themselves are meant to
[reflect](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/2026-star-ratings-fact-sheet.pdf)
43 or 33 measures of clinical quality, patient experience, and administrative
performance (there are more measures if the Medicare Advantage plan includes a
prescription drug benefit).

However, the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC)
[has](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-
content/uploads/import_data/scrape_files/docs/default-
source/reports/jun19_ch8_medpac_reporttocongress_sec.pdf)
[repeatedly](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-
content/uploads/import_data/scrape_files/docs/default-
source/reports/jun20_ch3_reporttocongress_sec.pdf)[over](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2026/03/Mar26_Ch12_MedPAC_Report_To_Congress_SEC.pdf#page=4)
the years lambasted the quality star program—even calling for its
abolishment—due to it being inaccurate, unreliable, and significantly
increasing government spending. For example, in March 2026, MedPAC
[summarized](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2026/03/Mar26_Ch12_MedPAC_Report_To_Congress_SEC.pdf#page=4)
in their report:

An excessive number of measures are assessed, and many administrative and
process measures are not reflective of the quality of care and/or experience
that plan enrollees can expect to receive.

MedPAC is not alone as several published analyses found that the measures
underlying the star ratings do
[not](https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2023-06/The%20Medicare%20Advantage%20Quality%20Bonus%20Program.pdf)
adequately and meaningfully separate the quality of different plans, and the
[creation](https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.2021.00606) of
the quality star system did not
[improve](https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/abs/10.1377/hlthaff.2025.00946)
key quality measures of plans.

To highlight some examples of glaring issues with the quality bonus program:
CMS [awards](https://medicare.chir.georgetown.edu/assessing-medicare-
advantage-quality-at-the-plan-versus-contract-level/) bonus payments at the
contract level, and insurers can include several, even hundreds, of plans in a
single contract. This effectively means, as MedPAC has
[noted](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2026/03/Mar26_Ch12_MedPAC_Report_To_Congress_SEC.pdf#page=4),
that the star rating for an entire contract can bear little to no resemblance
to patients’ experiences with their specific plans. Additionally, the
government has allowed insurers to combine contracts in a manner that inflates
their star rating and enables them to rake in higher bonus payments.

Additionally, the measures of “quality” are curious when zooming out to the
larger view of what constitutes successful health care coverage. Quality
measures [include](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/2026-star-ratings-
measures.pdf)but are not limited to whether patients get their annual flu
vaccine, whether they are screened for breast or colorectal cancer, and how
much they adhere to taking specific prescribed medications (ex: statins).
Another measure is [whether](https://healthalliance.org/documents/38648) they
received advice from a doctor in the past year on starting, increasing, or
maintaining their level of exercise.

These measures do not directly account for widely known quality issues with
Medicare Advantage and private insurance in the United States more generally.
Unlike traditional Medicare, private plans operate in
[restricted](https://cepr.net/publications/medicare-advantage-and-deceptive-
marketing/) networks, meaning that patients have much less choice in what
doctors they can see. Many providers
[have](https://www.medpagetoday.com/special-reports/exclusives/106483)
[stopped](https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/finance/16-health-systems-
dropping-medicare-advantage-plans-2026/) accepting Medicare Advantage plans
due to lower reimbursements and the administrative hassle of dealing with
private insurers. Administrative bloat is a feature of private insurance in
the United States, as both publicly-administered
[Medicare](https://cepr.net/publications/can-we-just-admit-were-wasting-money-
on-medicare-advantage/) and [Medicaid](https://cthealthpolicy.org/ct-medicaid-
admin-costs-are-5th-lowest-in-the-nation-but-ct-fully-insured-plans-are-
the-5th-highest/) have far lower administrative costs than their private
counterparts.

Insurance companies use prior authorization to delay and deny important care,
to the extent that 93 percent of 1,000 [surveyed](https://www.ama-
assn.org/system/files/prior-authorization-survey.pdf) physicians in 2024
reported that prior authorizations delayed access to necessary care always (15
percent), often (42 percent), or sometimes (36 percent). Additionally, 82
percent of physicians reported abandoning recommended care always (2 percent),
often (20 percent), or sometimes (60 percent).

Also, there is [little to no
evidence](https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2023-06/The%20Medicare%20Advantage%20Quality%20Bonus%20Program.pdf)
that Medicare Advantage plans use the quality bonus payments to improve their
coverage. This reality is not surprising. MA plans are significantly more
[profitable](https://www.kff.org/affordable-care-act/medicare-advantage-
insurers-report-much-higher-gross-margins-per-enrollee-than-insurers-in-other-
markets/) for insurance companies than their other types of offerings; yet,
insurers have repeatedly
[threatened](https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/regulatory/cms-proposes-flat-ma-
rates-risk-adjustment-updates-2027) to, and have
[actually](https://cepr.net/publications/new-research-reveals-millions-will-
lose-medicare-advantage-coverage-this-year/), cut benefits and plan offerings
when the government has moved to rein in overpayments.

Overpayments are a massive issue in the Medicare Advantage program, with
MedPAC [estimating](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/Jun26_MedPAC_Report_To_Congress_SEC.pdf) $76 billion
in taxpayer money unnecessarily going to insurance companies in 2026. This
follows $84 billion in [estimated](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2025/03/Mar25_MedPAC_Report_To_Congress_SEC-1.pdf)
overpayments in 2025, and MedPAC additionally
[estimated](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Tab-N-MA_Status-
Jan-2026.pdf) nearly half a trillion in overpayments for the period from 2020
to 2026.

These overpayments are a result of intentional strategies by insurance
companies to rip off taxpayers. Insurers make patients seem sicker than they
actually are — a practice called
[upcoding](https://cepr.net/publications/encouraging-crime-settlement-rewards-
medicare-advantage-fraud/) — which results in the government giving them
higher payments for each seemingly sicker patient. At the same time, these
companies engage in [favorable
selection](https://cepr.net/publications/alleged-kickbacks-further-expose-
medicare-advantage-corruption/): the practice of intentionally choosing
healthier patients that will require less money to cover. Insurers profit in
Medicare Advantage by getting as much money per patient as possible from
taxpayers and then spending as little as possible in covering care.

When patients need to utilize health care services more, or the government
potentially reins in overpayments to the extent that profits are reduced,
insurance companies can and have
[responded](https://cepr.net/publications/new-research-reveals-millions-will-
lose-medicare-advantage-coverage-this-year/) by eliminating plans and
decreasing the quality of others by offering fewer, worse benefits.

Simultaneously, the insurance lobby has been very
[effective](https://cepr.net/publications/corporate-power-protects-medicare-
advantage-fraud/) in stopping Congress and the Trump administration from
legislatively ending or even just limiting the tens of billions of dollars in
annual waste, fraud, and abuse. Congress has never voted on existing
[bipartisan](https://www.cassidy.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/cassidy-
merkley-introduce-bill-to-stop-overpayments-in-the-medicare-advantage-
program/) legislation to address upcoding, and this bill was
[excluded](https://www.beckerspayer.com/policy-updates/lawmakers-backtrack-on-
medicare-advantage-changes-in-budget-bill/) from the One Big Beautiful Bill in
2025 even though it was [introduced](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-
congress/senate-bill/1105) by Republican Senator Bill Cassidy. When CMS
[proposed](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/press-releases/cms-
proposes-2027-medicare-advantage-part-d-payment-policies-improve-payment-
accuracy-sustainability) to only increase the payment rate to insurers by 0.09
percent given the massive overpayments, insurance lobbyists got the Department
of Health and Human Services (HHS) to reverse course,
[increasing](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/press-releases/cms-
finalizes-2027-medicare-advantage-part-d-payment-policies-strengthen-
accountability-long-term) the payment rate by 2.48 percent. In Congressional
testimony, HHS Secretary Robert Kennedy, Jr. publicly
[admitted](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qiDUMsTZaH8) to such industry
influence.

This industry lobbying campaign succeeded even though both [Secretary
Kennedy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qiDUMsTZaH8)and [CMS administrator
Dr. Mehmet Oz](https://x.com/BrandonNovick/status/1900590958074273974) have
castigated the practice of upcoding, with Oz even calling companies that
upcode “scoundrels.” A clear indication as to why this campaign succeeded is
that seven of the largest insurance companies that offer MA plans
[spent](https://www.citizen.org/article/fact-sheet-largest-medicare-advantage-
firms-spend-big-to-influence-policy/) more than $330 million lobbying between
2020 and 2024. Public reporting has
[revealed](https://medicareadvocacy.org/cms-caves-to-medicare-advantage-
industry/) that this lobbying barrage included a focus on preventing the
government from cutting overpayments.

Given the reality of industry control of the federal government, it comes as
no surprise that CMS will hand an
[estimated](https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-will-spend-more-
than-13-billion-on-the-medicare-advantage-quality-bonus-program-in-2026/)
$13.4 billion in quality bonuses to Medicare Advantage plans in 2026, meaning
that the government will have given industry $50.7 billion in such bonuses
from just 2023 to 2026.

Ultimately, bipartisan members of Congress, MedPAC, the HHS Secretary, the
head of CMS, and independent researchers across the political spectrum have
all recognized the massive waste, fraud, and abuse in the Medicare Advantage
program. The only powerful actor in support of the current system is the
insurance industry itself. Yet, “somehow” policymakers have not fundamentally
changed any aspect of the Medicare Advantage program that would do away with
billions in stolen taxpayer dollars.

_This first appeared on[CEPR](http://www.cepr.net)._
